articles.title: South African white genocide does not exist, new ambassador to US tells BBC
articles.summary: Roelf Meyer tells the BBC that being a white Afrikaner gives him legitimacy to challenge Trump's claim of a genocide.
articles.byline: Ione Wells, Mayeni Jones, Ed Habershon

blocks.text: South Africa's new ambassador to Washington has a personal reason to challenge Donald Trump's assertion that there is a genocide against white Afrikaners - he is "a born Afrikaner" himself.
"Is he talking about us?", Roelf Meyer remembers thinking, when he first heard President Trump say it.
His response to the US president's claim is blunt.
The notion of a mass attack on the white Afrikaner minority in South Africa does not exist, he told the BBC, adding that his identity gave him the legitimacy to say so.

Meyer was one of the chief mediators to end white-minority rule known as apartheid in South Africa in the 1990s. He was appointed ambassador to the US in April, after diplomatic relations between the US and South Africa plummeted.

In an interview with the BBC, Meyer said the facts about violence in South Africa had been misrepresented and he never got a clear answer about where this "misdirection of information" was coming from.
Last year, Trump accused South Africa of white genocide in a meeting with President Cyril Ramaphosa at the White House and launched a US refugee pathway for Afrikaners.
Since last year, nearly 13,000 refugees were admitted to the United States and all but three were South African.
Among them was Lielie, the name she uses publicly, who moved with her family to Texas from South Africa, where they had lived on her stepfather's farm, growing macadamia nuts and bananas.
Despite walls around the house, an electric fence, and eight bull terriers, she said she felt "fear the whole time" and that on three occasions she saw people entering her property.
"Nothing was stolen, we weren't harmed, but there are friends of my husband, people that lived around us, they were brutally attacked," she said.
She said since moving to the US under the Trump administration's refugee pathway her life had changed, she felt safer walking around, and "my kids can actually play outside".
The Trump administration is planning to admit up to 17,500 additional white Afrikaners as refugees over the next 12 months, according to a notice sent to Congress on Tuesday.

In a statement to the BBC, a White House spokeswoman said: "President Trump has provided a lifeline for Afrikaners, who are being raped, maimed, killed and driven off their property across South Africa.

"While the South African government and many in the media have brushed off the horrific lived experiences of this community, the Trump administration continues to process applications for refugee status because the president has a humanitarian heart."
SJ Du Venage, who lives on South Africa's west coast, has been trying to move to the US under the new scheme.
Du Venage is a council member of the Freedom Front Plus, a right-wing Afrikaner party, and argues that there is a "political drive towards killing white people, and killing the farmers on the farms".
"There's absolutely an agenda to wipe us out here," he says.
An Afrikaner lobby group is holding a vigil on Saturday with thousands of white crosses on Washington's National Mall to commemorate what it says are victims of "farm attacks".
Claims of genocide against white South Africans have been discredited by every political party in the country, including by those representing Afrikaners.
"I'm an Afrikaner from South Africa myself," Ambassador Meyer said, "and I can say that I've never experienced something of that kind."
Meyer said he would like to have a conversation with Trump about the reality of the situation, saying that as a "born Afrikaner", he has the "legitimacy" to speak about the subject.

The ambassador helped negotiate an end to apartheid on behalf of the National Party, which was responsible for it, with now-president Cyril Ramaphosa also a key negotiator for the African National Congress party.
He said the "trust" between the two men was one reason President Ramaphosa appointed him to help mend US-South Africa relations, as well as "the fact he also saw the value of me being an Afrikaner".
"But I'm not here to represent the Afrikaner only," Meyer says.

Last week, the Trump administration announced visa restrictions for those South Africans who it said were responsible for "race-based discrimination" against white people. It also warned of further punitive actions if South African leaders did not address the issue.

Police data shows the majority of victims of crime in South Africa, including on farms, are black. Farm violence, often motivated by robberies, is an issue but represents a smaller number of homicides in the country.
While no politician disputes that crime is a problem in South Africa, many experts say this does not qualify as "persecution".

Larry Bartlett, the former director of the US Refugee Assistance Programme, said it could even be "unlawful" to appropriate a programme defined in law for people who "really have no chance to go home".
He said white people who were unlikely to qualify as refugee in law were taking scarce opportunities meant for those fleeing war or ethnic cleansing.

Alongside "rural safety", the Trump administration has raised other concerns about South Africa, including targets for companies to increase non-white employment and a law allowing the state, in exceptional circumstances, to expropriate land without compensation. These are aimed at redressing historic racial inequality.
Meyer wants Trump's executive order against South Africa, which underpins the refugee pathway, revoked.
He said South Africa had never prevented people from leaving and had addressed all the US concerns, stressing that the land expropriation law is awaiting a court judgement.
"South Africa has challenges with the prevention of crime and with the combatting of crime," he said.

But he added: "It's a problem all around. It's not rural. It's not farm attacks only. If you look at the total picture, the huge levels of crime in the black townships of South Africa are the biggest concern, proportionally, far more than anything else."
He said he would encourage the US to help South Africa with resources on combatting crime, including by providing equipment to speed up reaction times.
Meyer also has a message for Afrikaners protesting against "farm attacks" by laying white crosses in Washington.
"It doesn't help us to raise a voice outside, if we are not committed to doing something inside the country," he says.

articles.title: As Merz scrambles for support, Germany's identity crisis is laid bare
articles.summary: Voters are turning away from the centre in Germany as fears grow about the economy and migration.

blocks.text: A set of bumper local elections has thrown Germany, and its government, off balance.
Chancellor Friedrich Merz may now be a man on borrowed time. His coalition government is in crisis.
But this breakdown of business as usual in Germany has been brewing for years.
It's a nation wrestling with new, uncomfortable and unresolved realities.
Think of certain stereotypes about Germany, and think again.
A country dominated by boring, consensus-driven politics? Not any more.
A confident, powerhouse economy at the cutting edge of car-making? Yesterday's story.
A nation that can be used as a byword for impressive efficiency? The trains don't even run on time.
Many Germans I've spoken to feel their nation has drifted away from the things that once anchored their identity.
And the question of what next is, as yet, unanswered.
That uncertainty is currently embodied by a beleaguered chancellor weakened by bruising regional election results.
In the last fortnight, Friedrich Merz's party was beaten to first place in Berlin, pummelled in the polls in Saxony-Anhalt and pushed out of parliament altogether in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania.
A lifeline for Merz is that no-one, within his own centre-right CDU party, is yet willing to challenge the chancellor openly despite persistent rumours of a Kanzlertausch (chancellor swap).
But he is on thin ice, with record low approval ratings among voters who often describe him as arrogant and out of touch.
It is a problem that in government circles is sometimes more politely referred to as a "communication" issue.
Those who back the Chancellor say it is time to double down on much-needed reforms, alongside its centre-left SPD coalition partner, and find a better way of talking to people.
Swapping chancellors is not the answer as anyone would face the "same challenges", argues Jürgen Hardt, foreign policy spokesperson in parliament for Merz's CDU and its sister party, the CSU.

Hardt pointed out that the CDU/CSU fared far better in other regional elections earlier this year, when we spoke minutes after Merz addressed party lawmakers at a closed-door meeting in the Bundestag.

"I think Friedrich Merz knows about his deficits," says Hardt. "He will work on him and we will work on us as (a) party. And hopefully we will convince the people in the next months that we are on the right way."
Merz came to power in 2025, promising to get tough on immigration and boost Germany's ailing economy.
He appeared to offer a dynamism that might act as an antidote to the former dull, unhappy drumbeat of centre-left leader Olaf Scholz's bickering three-way coalition.
And Merz's allies would claim he has had some success.
This week, leading economic institutes raised the country's growth forecasts for 2026 and 2027 above 1% while illegal entries into Germany – and Europe – are down year on year.
But that will not eliminate public anxieties, on either issue.
Households and businesses continue to endure high energy costs while fears persist that China is cannibalising German industry, including its iconic car sector.
It is a brutal reversal of Germany's old recipe for success: cheap Russian gas that powered a booming export-driven economy.
And when it comes to immigration, the focus is now less on new arrivals and more on concerns about public safety, welfare costs and integration.
While there are local exceptions, voters appear to be losing faith in Germany's two principal governing parties (CDU and SPD).

Enter the rising force in German politics, Alternative für Deutschland (AfD): a party that alarms security officials with its Russia-friendly stance and contains regional branches that are classed as right-wing extremist by domestic intelligence.
Smears and misrepresentations, argues the AfD, as it claimed its third victory ever in a state election last Sunday in the north-eastern state of Mecklenburg-West Pomerania.
Its co-leader, Alice Weidel, told me this week that Friedrich Merz's days were numbered.

articles.title: Inside the FBI hack: Agents fearful and angry after 'dangerous' data breach
articles.summary: Current and former agents speak to the BBC about the devastating impact of the FBI hack.

blocks.text: Current and former FBI agents have spoken to BBC News of their shock, fear and anger following a hack that appears to have exposed the private and personal information of the agency's entire workforce.
"This is really bad for our undercover agents," says one former FBI agent, who fears for the safety of his colleagues.
The former cyber investigator is in a group chat with current agents who are worried their personal information could soon be freely available online to criminals and hostile nation-state hackers.
He says staff fear they could be targeted, or that criminals could use the data to create highly convincing phishing attempts, scams or demands for bribes.
The hacking group ShinyHunters is threatening to publish the stolen databases and documents within four days unless its demands are met.
Some agents are also concerned about the risk of physical attacks from cyber criminals they have investigated.
"One of the things we are discussing in the group chat is 'violence-as-a-service' attacks from young online gangs," says the former worker.
"They could use this information to harass an FBI agent who has worked on their cases."

Groups similar to ShinyHunters - believed to be an English-speaking gang - have in the past been linked to swatting incidents, and even petrol bomb attacks against law enforcement officers and rivals.
The group claims it breached FBI systems on Monday and later posted details of the attack on its darknet site.
The FBI has not responded to requests for comment.
However, on Wednesday the agency acknowledged the breach - saying it was "aggressively investigating" how it occurred.

For Michael McPherson, a former FBI agent who is now senior vice president of security operations at cyber firm ReliaQuest, the hack presents "a security threat which cuts to the core of agent safety, particularly their families".
He says agents understand the "inherent risks" that come with the job.

"But this incident reportedly includes personal data such as home addresses and contact information, which could expose family members who are normally insulated from the threats associated with such a career," McPherson says.
ShinyHunters shared samples of the alleged stolen data with reporters, along with an extortion demand.
The samples appear genuine and include names, addresses, phone numbers, badge numbers, job titles and information about spouses.
The records appear to relate to thousands of agents, including senior officials such as deputy directors.
The criminals also appear to possess highly sensitive medical information relating to thousands of special agents.

BBC News has seen samples of stolen "fitness-for-work" medical examinations containing information such as blood and urine test results, along with doctors' notes mentioning conditions including a "shellfish and banana allergy".
Agents' full names and addresses, as well as references to medical issues including "blood in the urine" and "high cholesterol" are now in the criminals' hands.

Cynthia Kaiser, who was the Deputy Director of Cyber at the FBI and now leads the Research Centre at Halcyon says ShinyHunters appear to already have lost control of some of the data which is circulating in various online groups of cyber researchers and could lead to harm even before the main tranche is published.
"A lot of the damage may already be done, and as we have seen in past FBI data breaches, that information continues to circulate the dark web years later," she said.
There are also concerns about the breach's national security implications, such as staff becoming targets for recruitment efforts by hostile foreign intelligence services.
Alongside fear, many of those who spoke to the BBC expressed anger at the FBI for allowing the data to be stolen.
The hack is particularly embarrassing from a technical perspective because ShinyHunters is not generally regarded as a highly sophisticated hacking group.
One former cyber agent said FBI staff were furious about the "sloppy and lazy security failures" that allegedly enabled the breach.
There is also confusion about how to handle any fallout if data is published next week, as threatened.
The FBI appears unlikely to comply with the extortion demands, and the hackers have indicated they intend to post the information on their darknet site.
Unusually, the group is not demanding money. Instead, it wants the FBI to retract an advisory published in May, which it claims "offended" them.
"The agency leadership is lost," the former cyber investigator tells me.
He says staff have been advised to sign up to a service called DeleteMe, which helps remove personal information from data broker websites - a response he feels is inadequate.

articles.title: Barangay, SK polls’ postponement draws mixed views in House
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — House of Representatives lawmakers were split on the enactment of a law that effectively suspends the 2026 Barangay and Sangguniang Kabataan Elections (BSKE), with Minority…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — House of Representatives lawmakers were split on the enactment of a law that effectively suspends the 2026 Barangay and Sangguniang Kabataan Elections (BSKE), with Minority members saying that the people would not benefit from this.

In a statement on Friday, Kabataan party-list Rep. Renee Co said that the basis for the enactment of Republic Act No. 12326, or the Act Fixing the Term of Office of Barangay Officials and Members of the Sangguniang Kabataan to Five Years — that foregoing an election will save funds amid a crisis — is flawed because the last polls were held in 2023 in the face of different societal problems.

In a social media post earlier, President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. confirmed that he has signed the law, which gives barangay officials five-year terms — and effectively setting the next BSKE to the second Monday of November 2028 and every five years thereafter.
This gave incumbent officials elected in 2023 an additional two years in their term.

“Ang karagdagang panahon sa panunungkulan ay karagdagang panahon para kumapit sa kapangyarihan, lalo na kung walang malinaw na batayan para ipagpaliban ang halalan. Kunwari pang term extension lang ang ginagawa, pero BSKE postponement ang totoong habol,” Co said.

(The additional two years in their term is an additional time to cling onto power, especially if there is no clear basis to delay the elections. They crafted it in the guise of term extension for barangay officials, but they are only after BSKE postponement.)

“Kung babalikan, naisagawa naman ang BSKE noong 2023 sa kabila ng iba’t ibang krisis, kaya malaking kasinungalingan kung sasabihin na hindi handa ang gobyerno. Sabi nga ng Comelec (Commission on Elections), gumastos na sila ng milyones sa paghahanda para sa paparating na eleksyon. Para saan pa ang lahat ng iyon kung hindi lang pala ito matutuloy?” she asked.

(If we can recall, the BSKE was held in 2023 despite different crises, that’s why it’s a big lie to say that the government is not prepared. As the Comelec (Commission on Elections) stated, they had already spent millions to prepare for the next elections. What is that for if the polls will not push through?)

Mamamayang Liberal party-list Rep. Leila de Lima believes the people would not gain from this decision, saying that she does not expect reforms to come out of the additional two years in the barangay officials’ term.
Instead, de Lima believes this additional time will only be used for politicking.

“Hindi taumbayan ang makikinabang sa paulit-ulit at niratsadang BSKE postponement. Bilyon-bilyong pondo na nagastos na ang masasayang. Ipagkakait na naman ang karapatan nating bumoto, at ang pagkakataong makapaglingkod ang marami pang karapat-dapat na lider – mga karapatan itong dapat igalang, hindi ine-etsapuwera o isinasakripisyo,” she said.

(The people would not benefit from the rushed BSKE postponement. Billions of funds spent will go to waste. They are depriving the people of our right to vote, and the chance to serve the rightful leaders of our communities — this is a right that must be respected, and not set aside or sacrificed.)
“Hindi reporma ang ibubunga ng paulit-ulit na BSKE postponement, kundi paglala ng mga perwisyong hatid ng sistemang padrino,” she added.
(Reforms do not come out of the repetitive BSKE postponement, but a worse menace brought by a padrino system.)
On the other hand, Manila Rep. Joel Chua, a member of the Majority, said that the resetting of the next elections gives incumbent barangay officials more time to serve their constituents.
“Wine-welcome namin ’yung naging desisyon ng ating Pangulo na i-postpone ang barangay election,” Chua, chairperson of the House committee on good government and public accountability, said on Friday.
(We welcome the decision of our President to postpone the barangay election.)
“Ito naman ay dagdag taon para sa mga opisyal ng barangay na kasalukuyang nakaupo. So, dagdag taon para sila po ay makapagserbisyo,” he added.
(This is an additional time for incumbent officials of the barangay. So it is also an additional year for them to serve well.)

Based on a copy of the law posted on the Official Gazette, incumbent elective barangay officials shall be considered to have completed one term in their respective positions, given the two-year extension of their terms.

“Incumbent officials serving their last term in the same position in accordance with Section 1 hereof shall be ineligible to run for the same position in the November 2028 Barangay and Sangguniang Kabataan Elections,” the law, which was officially signed on September 24, read.

A vacancy in the Sangguniang Kabataan shall be filled by appointment by the city or municipal mayor, while a vacancy in the SK chairperson position shall be filled through succession as provided by law.

Additionally, the law noted that being an incumbent official does not protect them from pending and future investigations concerning administrative, civil, or criminal cases or liabilities against them.

In a statement, Senator Francis Escudero thanked Marcos for signing the law, which he said would provide certainty and stability in governance—essential given that barangays serve as the government’s front line in delivering public services.
Escudero was the principal author of the bill’s version in the Senate.

This is not the first time that barangay elections were postponed under Marcos’ term. On October 12, 2022, the president signed a law that postpones the BSKE by a year, or from December 2022 to the last Monday of October 2023, and every three years after that.

However, this law was deemed unconstitutional by the Supreme Court (SC). In its ruling, the SC declared that the free and meaningful exercise of the right to vote, which is guaranteed by the Constitution, requires that elections be held at periodic intervals that are not unduly long.

SC said that while the original schedule of the elections had lapsed, their decision would serve as a guidance on the next elections. SC ordered that the October 2023 BSKE proceed, with the next elections held on December 5, 2025, and subsequent polls every three years after, on the first Monday of December.
Late opposition figure and former Albay lawmaker Edcel Lagman said in June 2023 that the SC decision supported their stand against the measure when it was still at the House.

Lagman said that SC’s decision affirms their contention that the reasons laid down by lawmakers who supported Republic Act No. 11935 — like the BSKE suspension being necessary for COVID-19 pandemic response and to avoid election fatigue — are “based on arbitrary grounds”.
Lagman was among the few lawmakers who opposed the proposal, saying as early as September 15, 2022 that the reasons for the BSKE suspension are not credible. /mr

articles.title: Two people arrested in New York City for allegedly climbing out of manhole
articles.summary:
Kevin Rodriguez and Samuel Reveron were booked after reports of ‘mole people’ emerging from sewers across city

Two people have been arrested for allegedly emerging from manholes across

blocks.text: Two people have been arrested for allegedly emerging from manholes across New York City.
Police reportedly suspect them of searching for valuables that had been washed into the storm drains and sewer system.
Kevin Rodriguez and Samuel Reveron, both 25, were arrested by New York City police on Friday and booked with counts of trespassing as well as conspiracy, the local news outlet WABC reported.

Court documents reviewed and reported by the outlet indicated that Rodriguez and Reveron were released without being required to post a bond because their charges were not eligible for a bail amount setting. According to court documents reviewed by WABC, Reveron got supervised release. WABC reported that Rodriguez was released on his own recognizance.
The New York Post reported that Reveron allegedly told police: “We go into the sewer and look for valuables that get stuck in the storm drains and sewers, gold, anything of value.

The arrests of Reveron and Rodriguez came after reports on Thursday that three people emerged from a manhole on Manhattan’s Upper East Side during the United Nations general assembly in New York City.
Three people were seen coming out from a sewer near Park Avenue and East 61st Street at about 4.35am on Wednesday before fleeing north on Park, according to WABC.

Officers responding to a 911 call about a possible crime learned of the situation after arriving near 535 Park Avenue. A New York City police surveillance camera captured the scene, according to the outlet, which cited officers.

A New York police spokesperson said the case met the “same criteria” as other recent ones involving “individuals going into the sewer system to look for valuables and other scrap metal after a storm”.
Police said they were “conducting additional security sweeps” with their federal partner “out of an abundance of caution given the UN general assembly and the sensitivity of the location”.
In late August, New York police said they were investigating a social media video of three people emerging from a manhole near Madison Square Garden.
That video came after a series of other reports of individuals – dubbed “mole people” by the hoi polloi – mysteriously emerging from manholes across Brooklyn and Queens.
Speaking to NBC New York in June, Aki Jakupovic, a witness, summarized the situation by remarking: “Three random guys walking around in a strange suit, open the sewer, go in like Ninja Turtles.”

articles.title: OpenAI says agents leaked 53 images from ChatGPT users in latest example of rogue activity
articles.summary:
Disclosure reveals ⁠new area of privacy risk for the company and illustrates ​how difficult it is to inventory unauthorized activity tied to its agents

Two ⁠months after OpenAI disclosed the…

blocks.text: Two ⁠months after OpenAI disclosed the accidental hacking of Hugging Face, the ChatGPT maker is still working to understand the full scope of its rogue agent activity, two people briefed on the matter told Reuters.

The latest example came on Friday when OpenAI said its agents had leaked 53 images from ChatGPT users. OpenAI declined to say if the images were AI-generated or identified real people. It also declined to ⁠say when the images were posted.

The disclosure reveals a ⁠new area of privacy risk for the company and illustrates ​how difficult it is even for an AI firm at the cutting edge of the technology to inventory all the unauthorized activity tied to its agents. OpenAI’s ongoing battle also reflects a yawning gap between the strength of the models the company is testing and its capacity to oversee or even track their actions.

As of mid-September, one person briefed on the matter estimated ⁠that OpenAI had found roughly two dozen incidents of its agents acting in undesirable ways. But the number has continued rising as OpenAI teams sift through internal logs of the agents’ activity and find previously unknown cases, the two people close to the company said.
OpenAI said its review would take “months” to complete given the scale of the work, and said it had notified “dozens” of third parties about improper activity.
Most of the leaked images have been ⁠taken down and OpenAI said it was lobbying hosting providers to remove the rest.

OpenAI’s agents had access to these images because the company relies on anonymized user data for part of its model-training process, according to the company, former employees and outside researchers. Enterprise data is not eligible for ​training, while ChatGPT consumers need to opt out of allowing the company to use their data for training.

Before user posts are ‌used for training, they go through an anonymization process that strips out ‌metadata, names and other contact information and should make it difficult to trace back to any individual user, the company said.

But the practice carries risks because there is a chance that the data may not be fully stripped of personally identifiable information and that it might ‌leak in the course of the model’s work, three people familiar with OpenAI’s practices said.

In the two months since OpenAI first announced that its agents broke containment, there have been more than 15 different OpenAI-related incidents of varying levels of severity disclosed by the company, by outside researchers, or – just on Wednesday – by Anthony Albanese, Australia’s prime minister, at the United Nations, who said OpenAI agents broke into a government health data portal in June.

The 21 July announcement that OpenAI’s agents had slipped out of control and hacked Hugging Face sparked widespread worries within the AI industry over its ability to control the more powerful AI models under development now. Since then, Anthropic, Alphabet’s Google and Meta have said they’ve found similar behavior by ​their agents after the Hugging Face incident prompted them to search.

OpenAI has acknowledged a general need for more transparency around rogue AI behavior. On 16 September, the company published a new framework for disclosing such incidents, saying it would err on the side of transparency “even when significance is uncertain”.
Even so, two people familiar with OpenAI’s investigation into its agents’ activity described it as locked down and shaped by company lawyers.
Roughly 100 people were in some way involved in the process to understand the Hugging Face hack, three people briefed on the matter said. During that process, evidence of other incidents surfaced.

Reuters has previously reported that OpenAI investigators looking into the Hugging Face breach were discouraged by the company’s lawyers from expanding the scope of the investigation to ⁠include other incidents. OpenAI said its lawyers did not discourage deeper investigation.
Many incidents have been uncovered by outside researchers rather than OpenAI directly. In several episodes, the agents took problematic actions that ​went unnoticed by the company for months.

Since the Hugging Face hack, researchers across the AI industry have grown worried that companies will not be able to predict or control their technology. Some have taken the path of Jacob Coxon, the former Anthropic researcher who publicly resigned this month in a viral social-media thread that said the AI labs are “gambling with our lives”.

In response to those concerns, Altman and his counterpart at Anthropic, CEO Dario Amodei, called for the industry to “pace” the development of AI and move cautiously in its pursuit of “recursive self improvement”. Altman doubled down on that message this week while addressing the United Nations.
Even so, both companies rolled out new models on Tuesday.

articles.title: OpenAI investigating 'dozens' of instances of agents acting improperly
articles.summary: OpenAI agents tried to get information from "governments, universities, public agencies, and other institutions" through extreme means that sometimes curbed security controls, the company said.

blocks.text: OpenAI said Friday it had alerted "dozens" of global institutions that their websites may have been impacted by its AI agents acting improperly.
OpenAI agents attempted to get information from "governments, universities, public agencies, and other institutions" through sometimes extreme means, the company said.

While some of the activity was simply due to the tools working to find "authoritative sources of public information," some went beyond that. Like an AI agent taking and transferring data when it should not have, OpenAI said.
Such activity resulted in at least 53 incidents where an OpenAI agent took an image from ChatGPT user activity and transferred it elsewhere.
The company said that in each instance of a user image being used and transferred by an AI agent, the user had allowed OpenAI to train models using their data.
Nevertheless, OpenAI admitted, "This is not an appropriate use of this data".
It added that the leak of user images occurred before it had put in place new safeguards on AI training, and it was working to get all the user images transferred to any third-party removed.
Reuters first reported these issues.

OpenAI also indicated on Friday that its software may have circumvented certain security controls of the sites impacted - though it doesn't necessarily mean each incident led to a significant security breach.

"Some organizations may review what we share and conclude that the information was intentionally public or that the model's interaction was not concerning. Others may identify a design issue or security weakness they want to address," the company said.

OpenAI said it came across the incidents during an investigation that started after it learned that its AI models had hacked the AI platform Hugging Face, an incident that was revealed publicly last month.

The disclosures on Friday comes just days after Australian's Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said OpenAI had breached non-public files on the website of its government-run health care scheme, Medicare.

articles.title: Supreme court blocks Trump-backed Missouri congressional map from use in midterms
articles.summary:
Court puts end to long-running legal dispute as it rules Republican-friendly map cannot be used in November

The supreme court on Friday turned away an attempt to use a new Missouri…

blocks.text: The supreme court on Friday turned away an attempt to use a new Missouri congressional map backed by Donald Trump, putting an end to a long-running legal dispute as absentee voting is under way in the midterm elections.

The justices halted a federal appeals court ruling that would have revived the Republican-friendly map for the November elections, which will determine control of Congress. There were no noted dissents.

The supreme court instead let stand a decision by the Missouri supreme court, which ruled earlier this month that a citizen petition prevents the new map from being used unless first approved by voters in a November referendum. The decision means Missouri residents will vote under the same congressional districts used in the 2024 and 2022 elections.

“At this late date, ordering reversion to the 2025 map in the midst of an ongoing election would usher in electoral chaos,” the high court wrote in an unsigned opinion. “The district court and court of appeals should not enjoin or otherwise prohibit the use of the 2022 map in the 2026 congressional election in Missouri.”

Republicans had hoped the new House map – which already was used in the August primaries – could help them win an additional seat as part of a nationwide redistricting battle pushed by Trump to gain an edge in the midterms.

A panel of the eighth US circuit court of appeals ruled on Monday that switching districts between the primary and general elections would violate the US constitution. The panel directed a district judge to bar Missouri from using anything other than the new map but delayed the order’s effect until next Monday to allow time for an appeal to the supreme court.

The legal wrangling has caused confusion for more than a million potential Missouri voters – nearly one in four statewide – who were shifted from one district to another, resulting in different candidates on their ballots. Absentee voting began Tuesday under the 2022 congressional districts, though some local election officials had urged voters to wait because of the legal uncertainty.

Republicans currently hold six of Missouri’s eight House districts. At the urging of Trump and Republican governor Mike Kehoe, Missouri lawmakers last September passed revised districts that were intended to help them win seven seats in the midterms.

The redistricting significantly reshaped a Kansas City-based district held by longtime Democratic congressman Emanuel Cleaver. It shed parts of Kansas City to neighboring districts with Republican incumbents and stretched the remainder of Cleaver’s fifth congressional district far eastward into rural Republican areas.

The result was about 59% of potential voters were new to the district, according to an Associated Press estimate. The ripple effects also shifted some voters in most of Missouri’s other congressional districts.

Cleaver was unopposed in the Democratic primary. Republican state senator Rick Brattin won a six-way Republican primary under the revised districts. They remain the candidates for the general election, even though the district boundaries have reverted to their prior lines.Brattin was a plaintiff, along with Republican congressman Bob Onder and two other voters, in a federal lawsuit that led to the eighth circuit’s ruling and the last two appeals to the supreme court.

At least 16 lawsuits have been filed in state and federal courts related to Missouri’s congressional redistricting. The battle has been the longest and most complex among roughly a dozen states that sought to change their US House districts over the past year.

Missouri’s new map survived most of the lawsuits, including ones contending that mid-decade redistricting violated the state constitution and that the new districts ran afoul of requirements to be compact . In one case, the Missouri supreme court allowed the new districts to be used while election officials worked to verify petition signatures seeking to put the map to a statewide vote.

Republican secretary of state Denny Hoskins waited until the legal deadline on 4 August – the day the new districts were used in the primaries – to reject the petition. He asserted referendum petitions aren’t allowed for congressional redistricting.

The Missouri supreme court ruled on 3 September that the referendum petition was valid. It ordered Hoskins not to use the new map and to instead use the districts adopted in 2022, after the last census. The supreme court let that ruling stand on 8 September. But minutes later, US district judge Stephen Clark issued a conflicting order in favor of the new map.

The supreme court on 10 September blocked Clark’s order from taking effect. That day, the Missouri supreme court held Hoskins temporarily in contempt for telling local election authorities to use the new map after Clark’s order.

But that wasn’t the end of the matter. The eighth circuit, hearing an appeal of Clark’s blocked order, ruled in favor of the Trump-backed map Monday. That’s what led to the latest decision from the US supreme court.

articles.title: Michigan CEO loses job after posting AI-made image of her family in ‘Lake America’ sweaters
articles.summary:
Jane Smith reportedly used ChatGPT to edit photo to show name Trump ordered US agencies to use for Lake Ontario amid trade war with Canada

The CEO of a

blocks.text: The CEO of a Michigan credit union is no longer employed there, according to the organization, after she posted on social media what appeared to be an AI-generated image of her and her family wearing sweaters emblazoned with the Donald Trump-associated words “Lake America”.
In the statement recently announcing that Jane Smith would no longer be its CEO, Family First Credit Union also apologized “for the concern, disappointment and pain this situation has caused”.

Smith had been the chief executive officer of the Family First Credit Union when she posed for a family photo at the Detroit airport en route to Halifax, Canada. She reportedly used ChatGPT to edit the family’s sweaters to say Lake America, which since late August has been the name that Trump ordered the US’s federal government agencies to use for Lake Ontario amid the president’s trade war with Canada.
Smith then shared the image on Facebook on 11 September – the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 terrorist attacks in the US – along with the caption: “Like our sweatshirts? Not sure Canada will.”
The post ended with “Lol lol”. It went viral and then provoked backlash from people in Canada – where a portion of the lake is.
Those online users found it disrespectful, and the post has since been deleted according to Canadian Broadcasting Corporation (CBC) News.

Many in the comments highlighted that the post was particularly insensitive, given Halifax’s role in hosting thousands of stranded airplane passengers who were diverted there when US airspace closed on the day of the 9/11 attacks.

As the controversy intensified, Family First Credit Union – based in Saginaw, Michigan – said it was reviewing the situation. Smith, meanwhile, apologized, expressing regret, maintaining that the post was the result of poor judgment and saying that she understood why it would be offensive.

“We weren’t trying to make a political statement,” Smith told the Detroit television news station WJRT. “However, we were, you know, kind of poking fun” at the changing of the name of one of the Great Lakes.

“I understand if I was someone in Halifax and I thought a poor group of people walked in wearing those sweatshirts, it is highly offensive and I would understand why they would be so angry,” she continued in her remarks to WJRT. “I am not a person that would ever want to offend or hurt anybody.
“I do regret having any post that would make someone feel like we don’t value them as human beings.”
Despite her apology, the credit union made it clear that it had parted ways with Smith.
“Jane Smith is no longer employed by Family First Credit Union, effective immediately,” said a statement from the organization shared on social media.

After saying Smith’s interim successor would be Jason Acosta, the statement continued, “We sincerely apologize for the concern, disappointment and pain this situation has caused our members and community.

“We understand that members of our community may hold different perspectives about this decision. Our responsibility is to act in the best interest of the Credit Union, uphold the trust of our members and continue putting our community first.”
Family First Credit Union’s statement about Smith came after broader repudiation in Canada and beyond of Trump’s executive order changing Lake Ontario’s name to Lake America.

Canada’s prime minister, Mark Carney, explained in a post on social media that the body of water’s name comes from the language of the Indigenous Wendat people – and predates both the Canadian Confederation and the US’s declaration of independence from the UK.
“Canadians … know that naming reality means calling it Lake Ontario – then, now and always,” he wrote on X.
Several US governors in the US’s Great Lakes region also dismissed the name change. Michigan borders the Canadian province of Ontario along with four of the five Great Lakes.
The only one of the Great Lakes that Michigan does not border is Lake Ontario. New York is the only US state that Lake Ontario borders.

Trump’s order has no authority to rename Canada’s portion of the lake. It also has no power to compel Canada, international legal bodies, international mapmakers or the rest of the world to adopt a new name.

articles.title: The treasured 'eternal snow' on this tropical island is about to disappear forever
articles.summary: Climate change is transforming Papua's snowy peaks, which hold scientific value and spiritual significance.

blocks.text: The treasured 'eternal snow' on this tropical island is about to disappear forever
Image source, Project Pressure/Klaus Tymann
Only small patches of snow remain on Papua's Sudirman Range
ByAbraham Utama
BBC Indonesia
The mountains of Papua are not far from the equator, but they've been topped with "eternal snow" for centuries.
The peaks in this Indonesian region on the world's second-largest island, just north of Australia, have offered scientists countless insights into the Earth's climate history.
They're also the epicentre of the spiritual universe for many Papuans - a Mecca or a Vatican, as one activist puts it.
But now, nearly all the snow is gone.
A century ago, the 300km (190-mile) stretch of the Sudirman Range had snow and permanent ice on all four of its major peaks.
But now there are only small areas around Puncak Jaya, also known as Carstensz Pyramid, with any snow at all. These are expected to entirely disappear in a year or two.

Glacier cover around the peak has shrunk from nearly 1,900 hectares (4,700 acres) in the 19th Century to about 16 hectares (40 acres) today. Almost entire glaciers have vanished within a human lifetime.

blocks.caption: Map and satellite image showing rapidly shrinking glaciers around Puncak Jaya in Indonesia's Papua region. Labels mark nearby peaks including Sumantri, Ngga Pulu and Carstensz East, with a callout noting that glaciers near the peaks are disappearing. An inset map locates Papua on the island of Ne…

blocks.text: "There is a profound unfairness in this," says Marie Šabacká, a Czech glacier ecologist who travelled to Puncak Jaya last March in a bid to be among the last scientists to study Papua's "eternal snow".

She says the tropical glaciers in Papua are unique because they are separated from other glacier systems by thousands of kilometres. Papua is home to the "last remaining tropical ice" between the Andes and Himalayas.
Ice cores taken from the slopes of Puncak Jaya preserve a record of climate history.

Scientists can use them to obtain information about atmospheric conditions in the region and understand changes in the planet's warmest ocean waters that surround the island - the tropical Pacific and Western Pacific Warm pool.
But this archive is disappearing before scientists have had time to fully study it.

blocks.caption: Image caption, The snow cover has reduced dramatically since this photo, taken in 1936

blocks.text: The snow cover has reduced dramatically since this photo, taken in 1936
Proof of a warming planet

The retreat of Papua's glaciers is driven by the same forces affecting ice around the world, Šabacká notes, a warming atmosphere caused by human activity, including the burning of fossil fuels like coal, oil and gas.
As temperatures rise, the freezing point moves higher up mountains, so more precipitation falls as rain instead of snow, even in places that once saw regular snowfall.
El Niño events can accelerate this process, while local factors such as cloud cover, snowfall and mountain topography influence its pace.
The mountains in Papua are just 450km (280 miles) south of the equator, where "permanent ice can survive only at very high altitudes and within a narrow range of climatic conditions", Šabacká says.
A small increase in temperature, a higher freezing point or shift from snowfall to rainfall can determine whether a glacier survives at all, she adds.
The glaciers' retreat is evidence the Earth has been warming over a long period - and their disappearance "removes both a biological habitat and part of a culturally significant landscape".

blocks.caption: Image caption, Šabacká, seen taking samples from Puncak Jaya, says Papua's vanishing glaciers are unique as they are so far from other glacier systems

blocks.text: Image source, Marie Šabacká
Šabacká, seen taking samples from Puncak Jaya, says Papua's vanishing glaciers are unique as they are so far from other glacier systems
A spiritual anchor
At least five groups of Indigenous people have had strong spiritual ties to Puncak Jaya for generations.
The Moni people refer to it as Mbainggela, and believe their ancestors watch over the mountain. To the Amungme people, the range is known as Nemangkawi, or the "White Arrow".

"Parents and grandparents prayed their children would have hearts like the White Arrow, never straying from the proper path," says Elfrida Natkime, a young Amungme woman. "It symbolises honesty, purity and moral integrity."
According to traditional Amungme beliefs, Nemangkawi symbolises how people should live.
Amungme environmental activist Adolfina Kum stresses how important the peak is to her people - and how traditions and cultural foundations risk being shattered as the ice melts.

"How would Muslims feel if Mecca were destroyed? How would Catholics feel if Rome or the Vatican were destroyed?" she asks. "For the Amungme people, that is what it feels like when Nemangkawi is destroyed."

blocks.caption: Image caption, The mountain holds immense spiritual significance for Indigenous people like Justinus, a man from the Moni tribe

blocks.text: The mountain holds immense spiritual significance for Indigenous people like Justinus, a man from the Moni tribe
For many Indigenous Papuans, the disappearance of the glacier is not an isolated event.
The discovery of vast copper and gold deposits transformed the region during the 20th Century, and the development of extractive industrial projects have reshaped parts of the landscape.
Entire mountain faces have been excavated and roads, industrial infrastructure and settlements have transformed surrounding valleys.

Papuans say the development has brought jobs, roads, education and economic opportunities, but also environmental degradation and decades of social conflict. Some have lost access to their ancestral lands as mining expanded.
The BBC has approached Freeport, which operates Papua's Grasberg mine, one of the world's largest gold and copper operations, for comment.

"Every time I see the mountains, I feel amazed, but I also feel sadness," says Elfrida Natkime. "Since the company came, I have seen the exploitation. But the development has also provided a livelihood for many people."

blocks.caption: Image caption, This 3D rendition by Klaus Thymann's Project Pressure shows where ice used to be in light blue

blocks.text: This 3D rendition by Klaus Thymann's Project Pressure shows where ice used to be in light blue
As local communities watch their sacred landscapes change, scientists and explorers are racing to document what is left.
Using drones and three-dimensional mapping techniques, Danish researcher Klaus Thymann and his team have created a detailed model of what remains.
From the early 2000s to 2025, the glaciated area has receded by 95%, he says. "There's almost no ice left. Those are the facts."
Thymann says glaciers are "incredibly powerful" as indicators of climate change.
"When people hear that something described as 'eternal' is disappearing, it triggers a reaction," he explains.
Adolfina Kum believes communities "lose an important source of strength" when sacred mountains, forests or ancestral places are disturbed.
"I often describe it as pulling out the roots of a tree. Once the roots are removed, the tree loses its foundation."

articles.title: Liberal MP says he was demoted for supporting NDP bill targeting arms export controls
articles.summary: Charlottetown MP Sean Casey says he was removed from his position as parliamentary secretary to the minister of veterans affairs because he voted against the government and supported an NDP private…

image.caption: Liberal MP Sean Casey says he was warned against voting for an NDP MP's bill that would tighten Canada's arms export rules. While over a dozen Liberals ultimately did, he was the only parliamentary secretary among them. (Sean Kilpatrick/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Politics·New

Charlottetown MP Sean Casey says he was removed from his position as parliamentary secretary to the minister of veterans affairs because he voted against the government and supported an NDP private member's bill that targeted arms export controls.
P.E.I. MP says he was warned that move would mean losing parliamentary secretary role
· CBC News
· Posted: Sep 25, 2026 5:31 PM EDT | Last Updated: 28 minutes ago

Charlottetown MP Sean Casey says he was removed from his position as parliamentary secretary to the minister of veterans affairs because he supported an NDP private member's bill that targeted arms exports to Israel.
In March, Casey said he was warned by the Liberal whip that if he supported NDP MP Jenny Kwan's Bill C-233, known as the No More Loopholes Act, then he would be relieved of his duties.
Although 15 Liberal MPs broke rank and supported the bill, Casey was the only parliamentary secretary to do so.

"The bill was targeted at closing the loopholes that allowed for Canadian military equipment to be sold to another country but end up in Israel, so end up being used to kill Palestinians," said Casey in an interview with CBC News.

items: NDP's U.S. arms-control bill fails, 15 Liberal MPs break rank with government
Crown corp. reviewed U.S.-bound arms exports over potential transfer to Israel

blocks.text: "That was the goal of the legislation. And that's what my constituents were concerned about."

Casey said he received a call from the Atlantic desk of the Prime Minister's Office (PMO) on Thursday saying that he was being replaced. He described the conversations with both the whip and the PMO as "direct" and clearly referencing his support for Kwan's bill.
On Friday, the PMO announced that Quebec MP Sophie Chatel will replace Casey.
Parliamentary secretaries make $20,900 above their base MP salary of $217,700 and represent the minister at public events.
Casey said over the past six months, he began to wonder whether he'd be disciplined at all.
"I kept my word to my constituents and I voted in favour of the legislation and didn't hear anything from anyone until yesterday," he said.
"It took so darn long, I was kind of wondering if they forgot about me."
Departure from Trudeau platform

Casey said his understanding was that Liberal MPs outside of cabinet were entitled to a free vote on private member's bills, except in cases that involve implementing the Liberal platform, traditional confidence matters like the budget or instances that affected protections guaranteed in the Charter of Rights and Freedoms.
This was explicitly laid out in the 2015 Liberal platform that brought the Trudeau Liberals to power.
"Based on everything I knew in my 15 years here, there was a rule change that was unbeknownst to me and to many of my colleagues," he said.

The Prime Minister's Office did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The vote did not appear to be whipped, given that more than a dozen Liberal MPs did support Kwan's bill, which ultimately failed.
In a statement, Kwan said what happened to Casey is "distressing and should concern all Canadians."
She said it raises questions about the Liberal government's commitment to allowing MPs to exercise their judgment and represent their constituents freely.
"The prime minister talks a good talk, but in reality, he will wield his power to shut down dissent," she said.

Casey said this will not prevent him from reflecting the will of his constituents in the House, saying "if anything, I'm freed a little bit to not have to toe the party line as strictly as is now apparently required."
But he said he continues to have "tremendous" respect for the prime minister and affection for the Liberal Party.
"What has happened doesn't change that one iota," he said.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Kate McKenna is a senior reporter with CBC’s parliamentary bureau in Ottawa, where she covers federal politics. She previously worked for CBC’s The Fifth Estate and in the Halifax, Montreal and Charlottetown newsrooms. Her investigative and breaking news coverage has won five RTDNA awards. She is the author of No Choice: The 30-Year Fight for Abortion on Prince Edward Island.

articles.title: Yemeni leader calls for general mobilization against Houthis
articles.summary: Amid military escalation with the Iran-backed Houthis, the Saudi-backed head of Yemen's governing body urged his compatriots to join the government forces.

image.caption: The civil war between the Saudi-backed Yemeni government and the Iran-backed Houthis has escalated sharply amid the Iran war Image: Marwan Abdullah Yahya Saeed Al-shabi/Anadolu/IMAGO

blocks.text: Rashad al-Alimi, the head of Yemen's Saudi-backed Presidential Leadership Council, on Friday called for a general mobilization in the war-torn country.

"I call upon the sons of our great people to engage in general mobilization and national mobilization, to rally around their armed and security forces," al-Alimi, who is also Supreme Commander of the Yemeni Armed Forces, said in a televised address.
The head of the governing body urged his compatriots to join the government forces weeks after Yemen's government was dealt a major blow by the Iran-backed Houthi rebels.

The Houthis have seized control of Yemen's entire Red Sea coast in a lightning offensive, allowing them to fully control the strategic Bab al-Mandab Strait, igniting global fears about shipping through the chokepoint.
What else did Yemen's leader say?

In his address, al-Alimi also said that the objective of the mobilization is to "restore state institutions and extend sovereignty over the entire national territory," including the Yemeni capital of Sanaa, which has been under Houthi control since 2014.
He added that anyone who defects from the Houthis to the government will be pardoned in an upcoming amnesty.
Al-Alimi addressed residents of Houthi-controlled areas, urging them to protect their children and not send them to fight alongside the Houthis.
"The state does not view you as a party to the conflict but as its people and partners," he said.
Why can't Saudi Arabia stop the Houthis?
Houthis escalate conflict

For more than a decade, the Houthis have been fighting Yemen's Saudi-backed government. Although a 2022 truce left the conflict largely frozen, fighting has recently flared up again amid the wider conflict involving Iran.

In recent weeks, the Houthis have intensified their missile and drone attacks on neighboring Saudi Arabia. They declared a maritime blockade and attacked Saudi targets in an attempt to stifle Saudi oil exports.
The Houthis accuse the kingdom of besieging Yemeni areas under their control. They attacked Riyadh for the first time in years over the weekend, marking a major escalation.

articles.title: Black woman found hanging from tree was dead before body was 'staged', police say
articles.summary: Tasia Fortune's body was found hanging from a tree on the grounds of an abandoned home in Jackson in August.

blocks.text: Warning: This story contains distressing details
Police in the US state of Mississippi have said that they believe a black woman was already dead before her body was "staged" and placed hanging in a tree.
The disclosure was made in court by a detective on Friday, who also said they believed Tasia Fortune, a mother of four, had been killed in a dispute related to drugs.
The 29-year-old's body was found hanging from a tree on the grounds of an abandoned home in Jackson in August.

The discovery sparked widespread fears in the majority-black city, due to the state's deep history of racial violence and lynchings. After weeks of speculation and demands for information, police made multiple arrests.
In a news release, police said that the medical examiner had determined after an autopsy that Fortune's death was a homicide and that "the scene and the hanging were staged".
The BBC has contacted the court, the medical examiner's office and Fortune's mother, Christy Spivey.
Officials have not stated the exact cause of death or shared why they believe the hanging was staged.
The medical examiner confirmed earlier this month that Fortune's cause of death was homicide and said there would be a murder charge.
Speaking to reporters outside the Jackson Police Department on Friday, Fortune's mother described how she knows her daughter fought for her life till the very end.
"I know she did. I know my daughter," Spivey told reporters. Fortune leaves behind four young children, ages 7, 5, 4 and 1, she added.
Dressed in a shirt that reads "Justice for Tasia Fortune", Spivey stressed that she does not want to see any innocent people going to jail.
"I just hope they have the right people," she said.
Three people have been arrested in relation to the case, including Jarques Ratliff, 51, who was arrested and pleaded not guilty. He remains in custody in without bond.
A second person, Earnest Lloyd Jr, 25, was arrested in the case this week.
A third, 45-year-old Eric Clark, turned himself in to authorities on Friday and was charged with murder. He is scheduled to appear in court on Monday.

The 29-year-old's death is one of several cases in recent years that has prompted lawmakers to call on the justice department and the FBI to investigate all hanging deaths of black people in the country.
Representative Ayanna Pressley, Democrat of Massachusetts, cites at least 10 documented incidents in her September letter to Congress, external, which contained over 50 signatures from US lawmakers.
The most recent incident happened in Prince George's County, a majority-black suburb near Washington DC, on Sunday. It has been ruled a suicide.

articles.title: Ed Sheeran’s shows at Robert Kraft’s Gillette Stadium cancelled due to bad weather
articles.summary: Ed Sheeran’s concerts at Gillette Stadium in Massachusetts have been cancelled due to severe weather warnings, the latest blow to a tour that has been surrounded by controversy since opener…

image.caption: Ed Sheeran, shown here performing during iHeartRadio KISS108's Jingle Ball 2025 in Boston, Massachusetts, will no longer be performing at Gillette Stadium in Massachusetts this weekend due to bad weather. (Paras Griffin/Getty Images for for iHeartRadio)

blocks.text: Entertainment·New

Ed Sheeran’s concerts at Gillette Stadium in Massachusetts have been cancelled due to severe weather warnings, the latest blow to a tour that has been surrounded by controversy since opener Macklemore was dropped for his pro-Palestinian comments on stage.
Cancellations are latest blow to Sheeran's tour

Ed Sheeran’s concerts at Gillette Stadium in Massachusetts have been cancelled due to severe weather warnings, the latest blow to a tour that has been mired in controversy since opener Macklemore was dropped for on-stage pro-Palestinian comments.

Earlier this month, Macklemore was dropped from the tour's U.S. leg after stadium owners including billionaire Robert Kraft threatened to cancel Sheeran's shows if the rapper remained on the lineup, triggering an exodus as Sheeran’s remaining openers pulled out in solidarity.

Now, Sheeran will no longer be performing at Kraft’s Gillette Stadium on Friday and Saturday. Local weather reports are calling for a storm with gusts of wind up to 64 kilometres per hour in Foxborough, where the stadium is located, outside of Boston.

“Due to the severe weather warnings in place in Boston and across New England throughout the weekend and following consultation with local officials, we have made the difficult decision to cancel the Ed Sheeran concerts at Gillette Stadium,” Messina Touring, Sheeran’s touring group, said in an Instagram statement. The venue shared the same statement.
All tickets will be refunded through their point of purchase, the touring group added.

The cancellation comes a day after Macklemore announced a new tour of his own, with proceeds going to organizations supporting Palestinians. He slammed what he called “the billionaire class” deciding “which voices are allowed on stage and which ones are too dangerous to hear,” quipping that his schedule had recently “freed up a bit” since being dropped as an opener.
"It’s 2026. Being apolitical during a genocide doesn’t work anymore," he wrote.
An independent UN commission and Amnesty International have concluded that Israel's actions against Palestinians in Gaza amount to genocide, which the country has consistently denied.
Macklemore played 2 shows before being dropped

Before being pulled from the roster, Macklemore had played two shows in early September at New Jersey’s MetLife Stadium for the U.S. leg of Sheeran's Loop Tour. In speeches during those sets, he chanted, “Free Palestine” to a cheering crowd and expressed solidarity with Palestinians in Gaza and the Israeli-occupied West Bank.

Kraft, owner of the New England Patriots and their home base Gillette Stadium, was one of those behind the push for Macklemore’s removal, according to Messina, Macklemore and Sheeran, who said he spoke on the phone with Kraft during discussions about the push to remove the rapper.
Sheeran has said the decision was solely due to venues and promoters, and that they would not change their minds.
In a statement about Macklemore's removal, Sheeran said he was "appalled by the conflict" but defended his choice not to take a public stance.

items: Macklemore announces new tour in support of Palestine
Why Ed Sheeran's response to the criticism fell short
Ms. Rachel pledges $1M US in Palestinian aid to match Macklemore's donation following Sheeran tour exit

blocks.text: Kraft told CBC News in a statement at the time that due to Macklemore’s New Jersey shows and “a broader history of antisemitic rhetoric,” he believed performances at Gillette Stadium would “cross that line.”
The rapper was also widely criticized in 2014 for wearing a Halloween costume that many said was antisemitic. He apologized for the incident at the time.
Openers Lukas Graham, Aaron Rowe and Finneas pulled out of the tour after Macklemore’s ousting, as did Sheeran’s backing band, Irish group Beoga.
“We should be able to speak about war, about civilians being killed.… Money doesn’t give you the right to own the conversation,” Graham wrote on Instagram.
Fans seeking refunds
The Gillette tour dates would have been Sheeran's second and third shows since losing his supporting acts.

At his first show without the acts on Sept. 19 at Lincoln Financial Field in Philadelphia, Sheeran apologized to the crowd, saying he never wanted to be an "activist musician" and that "what is happening in Gaza is catastrophic and unjustifiable." He added that he is "listening and learning."

Pro-Palestinian protesters outside the venue called on other fans to boycott the show, criticizing Sheeran's apolitical stance. Prices have also sagged for remaining tickets since the controversy began.
Prior to the total cancellation of the Massachusetts shows, the state's attorney general had said that consumers looking for refunds due to the lineup changes would be granted them.

“After hearing from nearly 200 consumers who were struggling to obtain refunds from Ticketmaster for Ed Sheeran’s shows at Gillette Stadium this weekend, my office jumped into action to demand that consumers be provided a clear path to get their money back if they no longer want to attend due to significant changes to the lineup,” Andrea Joy Campbell said in a statement.

Ticketmaster's policy allows for openers to change without requiring that audiences be eligible for refunds. But Campbell said after her office submitted a request to the company, it made an exception for the Sept. 25 and 26 shows.
Did Ed Sheeran’s concert statement meet the moment?
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Alexandra Mae Jones is a senior writer for CBC News based in Toronto. She has written on a variety of topics, from health to pop culture to breaking news, and previously reported for CTV News and the Toronto Star. She joined CBC in 2024. You can reach her at alexandra.mae.jones@cbc.ca

articles.title: Hawaii readies for arrival of Hurricane Nolo amid risks of catastrophic flooding
articles.summary: Residents on Hawaii's Big Island were bracing Friday for potentially life-threatening and catastrophic flooding from Hurricane Nolo, while Mexico was still under the threat of Hurricane Polo as it…

image.caption: Ryanna Fry takes a picture of clouds in Kona, Hawaii, on Friday. Residents on Hawaii's Big Island were bracing Friday for potentially life-threatening and catastrophic flooding from Hurricane Nolo. (Gregory Bull/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World·New

Residents on Hawaii's Big Island were bracing Friday for potentially life-threatening and catastrophic flooding from Hurricane Nolo, while Mexico was still under the threat of Hurricane Polo as it headed toward the Baja Peninsula after bringing storm conditions to the southwestern coast.
Mexico remains under threat from Hurricane Polo as it heads toward Baja Peninsula

Nolo's maximum sustained winds have increased to 165 kilometres an hour, making it a Category 2 hurricane. The storm's centre was located about 300 kilometres south of South Point, Hawaii and about 610 kilometres south-southeast of Honolulu. It was moving north-northeast at about eight kilometres an hour.

Tropical storm conditions expected to begin on land in the evening, with hurricane conditions possible by early Saturday, the U.S. National Hurricane Center said. It was expected to take a turn west Saturday and avoid directly hitting the islands.
Forecasters warned eastern and southern areas of the island could see rainfall totals of 25 to 38 centimetres, with a maximum of 64 centimetres. Wind gusts on land could hit 80 kilometres an hour.
Nolo was expected to strengthen to a major hurricane on Saturday.

"People are going to want to kind of shelter in place on the Big Island, be in their safe place, certainly by later today, tonight, well into Saturday," Michael Brennan, director of the National Hurricane Center, said Friday.
"Don't venture out if you don't have to into the dangerous flooding environment, but also high winds. We can have trees and power lines down."
Heavy rainfall possible elsewhere
Heavy rainfall also was possible on Hawaii's other islands, the hurricane centre said. Maui also could see heavy rainfall and potential life-threatening flooding and mudslides, forecasters said.

Crews on the Big Island spent hours Friday trying to build berms to guide water and move large debris ahead of the worst of the rain, said Erika Kapu, Hawaii program manager for the humanitarian non-profit CORE.

Hawaii officials told residents to put together emergency kits and the governor issued an emergency proclamation, activating more than 230 Hawaii National Guard members. Schools were closed in some areas.

Hawaii County officials on the Big Island were urging residents in flood-prone areas to consider taking refuge at shelters being set up or other locations. Authorities said sand for sandbags was publicly available at several locations.

items: Southwestern Mexico braces for arrival of 'extremely dangerous' Hurricane Polo

blocks.text: The heaviest rain from Nolo is likely to fall over the same southeastern region of the Big Island that was hit in August by Hurricane Lala and where grounds are still wet from additional precipitation. The storm surge could hit 30 to 91 centimetres, creating large and dangerous waves and coastal flooding, the hurricane centre said.
Residents and tourists on the Big Island were busy preparing.
"I guess that'd be my concern — whether we're getting out of here or not, but, you know, as far as the weather goes, it is what it is," said Daniel Compton, who was visiting from Seattle.
Hawaii Gov. Josh Green has requested an emergency disaster declaration for four Hawaii counties.
Polo gaining strength

The hurricane centre said Polo gained significant force overnight into Friday morning and doused parts of Mexico's Pacific coast. No major damage or flooding was reported along the coast overnight into Friday.

By midday Friday, attention turned to the Baja California Peninsula, where the hurricane was slated to arch back and hit between Monday and Tuesday. Local authorities were preparing shelters. Mexico's government announced Friday afternoon that they were closing ports in the region as dark clouds swirled overhead.
The latest estimated sustained winds were 290 kilometres an hour.

Residents stacked sandbags to fortify beachfront shops and evacuated their homes in some coastal areas on Thursday. Mexican authorities opened shelters and cleared people from beaches, and 15,000 security personnel were deployed across the coast. Schools were closed.

In the port city of Lázaro Cárdenas in Michoacán, seawater swept through homes and left wooden planks and furniture strewn on the streets. Locals and government officials were clearing debris and shoveling thick mud coating much of the town.

Alicia Contreras said the walls and roof of her restaurant had been severely damaged by 4.5-metre waves. As officers and family helped pick through the damage, Contreras worried about how she would recover economically.
"This is huge because we have no other source of income. Now we're just surviving," Contreras said.

Brennan said some moisture associated with Polo will be pushed into parts of the southwestern U.S. by Monday, possibly producing scattered flash flooding in the Four Corners region, particularly portions of Arizona and New Mexico.
El Niño prompts global shifts

El Niño is prompting major environmental shifts across the world, fuelling drought in some areas and flooding in others. It traditionally dampens the Atlantic hurricane season, while it tends to rev up tropical cyclone activity in the Pacific with moist air and little wind shear.
A third storm in the Pacific, Hurricane Odalys, was at Category 4 status and was still far from land, roughly 1,537 kilometres west-southwest of the southern tip of the Baja California peninsula.
LISTEN | Will our weather always be like this?:
What on Earth?25:02Is this Super El Niño a peek into forever weather?
Two other powerful storms were churning in the Atlantic Ocean, but were not near land.

In the northern Atlantic, Tropical Storm Fay reformed early Thursday. As of Friday, it was about 1,674 kilometres west-southwest of the Azores, the hurricane centre said. Off Africa's western coast, Tropical Storm Gonzalo strengthened early Friday as it approached the Cabo Verde Islands.
